soft.text: Salmonella in ingredients added after the cook step is not analyzed / The cook is the only kill step, and it treats only the beans. Tahini, garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and spices go in at blending, after the kill step. Tahini and spices have well-known Salmonella history. The hazard analysis lists tahini only for sesame, so nothing in the plan controls Salmonella coming in with those ingredients. / Add a hazard analysis row for each ingredient added after the cook (at least tahini, spices, garlic and lemon juice) that considers Salmonella and other pathogens. Then name the control. Usually this is a supply-chain-applied control, meaning the supplier treats the ingredient and you verify it; see the supply-chain gap below. / 21 CFR 117.130(b) and (c) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / page 3, section 3 Hazard analysis / inferred / Cook step is the kill step for the finished product

Chemical hazards other than sesame not evaluated / The rule requires the hazard analysis to consider biological, chemical (including radiological) and physical hazards. The only chemical hazard in the table is the sesame allergen. Sanitizer and cleaning chemical residues, pesticide residues and mycotoxins in beans or tahini, and any other allergens in the building are not considered, not even to rule them out. / Add rows for each reasonably foreseeable chemical hazard with a yes/no decision and a reason, even when the answer is no. / 21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / page 3, section 3 Hazard analysis / inferred

Refrigerated storage hazard has no preventive control / The hazard analysis says Listeria growth in refrigerated storage needs a preventive control. But section 4 has no control for it, section 5 does not monitor cooler temperature, and section 6 has no corrective action for a cooler going above temperature. Section 1 already names the limit (at or below 41°F). / Add a refrigeration control (product held at or below 41°F), continuous or scheduled cooler temperature monitoring with a named person responsible, and a corrective action for temperature excursions that includes evaluating the product. / 21 CFR 117.135, 117.145, 117.150 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / page 3 (hazard row) vs. pages 4–5 (sections 4, 5, 6) / read / Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

A metal detector does not find stones, and section 4 lists no stone control. There is no sorting, destoning or visual inspection step in the process flow. / Either add an in-plant control (a destoner, sorting or a visual inspection step with monitoring) or treat supplier cleaning as a supply-chain-applied control covered by the Subpart G program. / 21 CFR 117.135; Subpart G if supplier-controlled / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / page 3, row 'Receiving dry beans'; page 4, section 4 / read / Field debris in dry beans, controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening

soft.text: Supply-chain program is too thin / Section 8 is two sentences: suppliers need an audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The plan itself relies on 'supplier screening' for field debris, and inferred Salmonella controls in tahini would also sit with suppliers. When a supplier controls a hazard, the rule requires a written program. It must cover supplier approval, the verification activities chosen for each supplier and why, onsite audits by a qualified auditor (annually by default where the hazard could cause serious illness or death, as Salmonella can), review of audit results, and the matching records. A certificate alone is not the audit report the rule requires you to review. / Expand section 8. For each ingredient controlled by a supplier, name the hazard and the supplier's control, record how the supplier was approved, and set the verification activity and how often it happens (for example, an annual onsite audit report reviewed by the PCQI, plus COA review with Salmonella results). Add the records kept under 117.475. / 21 CFR Part 117 Subpart G (117.405–117.475), in particular 117.410, 117.420, 117.430(b), 117.475 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-G / page 6, section 8 Supply-chain program / inferred / Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

No validation of the cook and cooling limits / Process controls must be validated by or under a PCQI to show they actually control the hazard. The plan states the cook and cooling limits but never cites the science behind them or says validation was done. / Add a validation statement for the cook and cooling steps, citing the scientific basis (for example, FDA Food Code cooling parameters and published legume cook lethality data) or an in-plant study, and keep the validation file. The statement can be written now; the evidence has to exist. / 21 CFR 117.160 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / not in the document (belongs in section 7 Verification) / read

Records review leaves out calibration, testing and supplier records / The PCQI's review covers monitoring records (cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen, metal). The rule also requires timely review of calibration records, product and environmental test results, and supplier verification records. The plan does not name these. / Extend the section 7 review to thermometer calibration, metal detector service records, product and environmental test results, and supplier verification records, with a time frame for each. / 21 CFR 117.165(a)(4)(ii) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / page 6, section 7 Verification / read / The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

No reanalysis schedule or triggers / The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every three years, or when something changes (a new product, supplier or process, new hazard information, or a failed control). A written statement is not strictly listed among the required plan contents, but the reanalysis itself is required. / Add a short section stating reanalysis at least every three years and on the listed triggers, performed or overseen by the PCQI. / 21 CFR 117.170 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / not in the document / inferred

identity.title: FSMA Food Safety Plan (Preventive Controls for Human Food): ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips, Salem Plant
identity.issuer: Willamette Valley Foods, Inc. (prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager and PCQI)
identity.site: Salem — 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301

scan.summary: This is the plant's written food safety plan, required by FDA's Preventive Controls for Human Food rule (21 CFR Part 117, Subpart C). It is the company's own document, so gaps in it are yours to close before an FDA or Oregon Department of Agriculture inspector finds them. The core is solid: a hazard analysis, cook and cooling limits, Listeria environmental swabbing, sesame labeling and scheduling, and metal detection. But it is missing a recall plan and the owner's signature, and it never looks at Salmonella in the tahini and other ingredients that go in after the cook step. That third gap is the most serious.
scan.freshness_note: The plan took effect May 12, 2025, so it is about 16 months old. It is not stale, but FDA requires a full reanalysis at least every three years (by about May 12, 2028 — inferred), and sooner if a product, process, supplier or hazard changes. If anything has changed since May 2025, such as new flavors, new suppliers or new equipment, ask whether a newer version exists.

gaps.title: No written recall plan
gaps.description: A plan with hazards that need preventive controls must include a written recall plan. There is none here. That means nothing on notifying the retailers who receive the product, telling the public, running effectiveness checks, or disposing of recalled product.
gaps.fix: Write a recall plan and add it as a new section. It should cover who decides on a recall, how customers in Oregon, Washington and Idaho are notified, how the public is told when needed, how effectiveness is checked, and what happens to returned product. Hold a mock recall to test it.

gaps.title: Plan not signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge
gaps.description: The cover page names a job title as approver, but there is no name, no signature and no date. FDA requires the owner, operator or agent in charge to sign and date the plan when it is first completed and after every change.
gaps.fix: Have the plant manager (or owner) sign the plan with their printed name and the date. Add a signature and date block for each future revision.

gaps.title: Salmonella in ingredients added after the cook step is not analyzed
gaps.description: The cook is the only kill step, and it treats only the beans. Tahini, garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and spices go in at blending, after the kill step. Tahini and spices have well-known Salmonella history. The hazard analysis lists tahini only for sesame, so nothing in the plan controls Salmonella coming in with those ingredients.
gaps.fix: Add a hazard analysis row for each ingredient added after the cook (at least tahini, spices, garlic and lemon juice) that considers Salmonella and other pathogens. Then name the control. Usually this is a supply-chain-applied control, meaning the supplier treats the ingredient and you verify it; see the supply-chain gap below.
gaps.quote: Cook step is the kill step for the finished product

gaps.title: Chemical hazards other than sesame not evaluated
gaps.description: The rule requires the hazard analysis to consider biological, chemical (including radiological) and physical hazards. The only chemical hazard in the table is the sesame allergen. Sanitizer and cleaning chemical residues, pesticide residues and mycotoxins in beans or tahini, and any other allergens in the building are not considered, not even to rule them out.
gaps.fix: Add rows for each reasonably foreseeable chemical hazard with a yes/no decision and a reason, even when the answer is no.

gaps.title: Supply-chain program is too thin
gaps.description: Section 8 is two sentences: suppliers need an audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The plan itself relies on 'supplier screening' for field debris, and inferred Salmonella controls in tahini would also sit with suppliers. When a supplier controls a hazard, the rule requires a written program. It must cover supplier approval, the verification activities chosen for each supplier and why, onsite audits by a qualified auditor (annually by default where the hazard could cause serious illness or death, as Salmonella can), review of audit results, and the matching records. A certificate alone is not the audit report the rule requires you to review.
gaps.fix: Expand section 8. For each ingredient controlled by a supplier, name the hazard and the supplier's control, record how the supplier was approved, and set the verification activity and how often it happens (for example, an annual onsite audit report reviewed by the PCQI, plus COA review with Salmonella results). Add the records kept under 117.475.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: Refrigerated storage hazard has no preventive control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says Listeria growth in refrigerated storage needs a preventive control. But section 4 has no control for it, section 5 does not monitor cooler temperature, and section 6 has no corrective action for a cooler going above temperature. Section 1 already names the limit (at or below 41°F).
gaps.fix: Add a refrigeration control (product held at or below 41°F), continuous or scheduled cooler temperature monitoring with a named person responsible, and a corrective action for temperature excursions that includes evaluating the product.
gaps.quote: Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Stones in dry beans have no working control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis marks stones and metal in dry beans as needing a preventive control, controlled 'at metal detection and by supplier screening.' A metal detector does not find stones, and section 4 lists no stone control. There is no sorting, destoning or visual inspection step in the process flow.
gaps.fix: Either add an in-plant control (a destoner, sorting or a visual inspection step with monitoring) or treat supplier cleaning as a supply-chain-applied control covered by the Subpart G program.
gaps.locator: page 3, row 'Receiving dry beans'; page 4, section 4
gaps.quote: Field debris in dry beans, controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening

gaps.title: No validation of the cook and cooling limits
gaps.description: Process controls must be validated by or under a PCQI to show they actually control the hazard. The plan states the cook and cooling limits but never cites the science behind them or says validation was done.
gaps.fix: Add a validation statement for the cook and cooling steps, citing the scientific basis (for example, FDA Food Code cooling parameters and published legume cook lethality data) or an in-plant study, and keep the validation file. The statement can be written now; the evidence has to exist.
gaps.locator: not in the document (belongs in section 7 Verification)

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring procedure is incomplete
gaps.description: The plan says 10 Listeria spp. swab sites weekly in zones 1 and 2. The written procedure must also identify the sampling locations, when during production samples are taken, the test method and the laboratory. None of these is stated.
gaps.fix: Attach or reference a site map with named swab sites and rotation, the time of sampling (for example, 3+ hours into production), the test method and the lab.
gaps.quote: Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2

gaps.title: Finished product testing: no procedure and no response to a positive
gaps.description: The plan tests finished product monthly for Listeria monocytogenes. It does not say how samples are drawn, which method is used or which lab runs it. Section 6 does not say what happens if product tests positive, and that response is a required corrective action procedure.
gaps.fix: Write the sampling plan, method and lab into section 7. Add a corrective action to section 6 for a positive product result: hold or recall affected lots, investigate the cause, intensify swabbing and document it all.
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: Corrective actions skip root cause and product evaluation
gaps.description: The rule requires corrective actions to find and fix the cause, reduce the chance it happens again, evaluate affected food for safety, and keep bad product out of commerce. Only the cook deviation says the cause is recorded. For metal detector failures, label mismatches and cooling failures, the plan does not ask why it happened. The label mismatch step only quarantines the label lot and does not check product that may already carry the wrong label.
gaps.fix: Add one general sentence to section 6 requiring, for every deviation, a cause investigation, action to prevent it happening again, and a safety evaluation of affected product. Add a check of already-labeled product to the label mismatch step.
gaps.quote: If a label does not match the formulation, the lot is quarantined and not used.

gaps.title: Allergen label check at printing and on the line not monitored
gaps.description: Section 4 says labels are reviewed at receipt and at printing. Section 5 monitors only the check at receipt. Nothing verifies that the right label goes on the right product during packaging, and that is where most undeclared-allergen recalls start.
gaps.fix: Add monitoring of the label check at printing and a label-to-product check on the line at start-up and at each product changeover, recorded on the label log.
gaps.quote: The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log.

gaps.title: Records review leaves out calibration, testing and supplier records
gaps.description: The PCQI's review covers monitoring records (cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen, metal). The rule also requires timely review of calibration records, product and environmental test results, and supplier verification records. The plan does not name these.
gaps.fix: Extend the section 7 review to thermometer calibration, metal detector service records, product and environmental test results, and supplier verification records, with a time frame for each.
gaps.quote: The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

gaps.title: No reanalysis schedule or triggers
gaps.description: The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every three years, or when something changes (a new product, supplier or process, new hazard information, or a failed control). A written statement is not strictly listed among the required plan contents, but the reanalysis itself is required.
gaps.fix: Add a short section stating reanalysis at least every three years and on the listed triggers, performed or overseen by the PCQI.

scan.confidence_notes: The file is clean, typed text, and I read all 7 pages. I am confident on what is in and out of the document, and on the required plan contents under 21 CFR 117.126(b): hazard analysis, preventive controls, supply-chain program, recall plan, monitoring, corrective actions and verification. The missing recall plan and the missing owner signature and date (117.310) are clear. The Salmonella-in-tahini finding and the supply-chain finding are inferred: they rest on the process flow showing tahini and spices added after the cook, and on the known history of those ingredients. Your PCQI could document a different control, but the plan has to say so. On FSMA 204, secondary sources say the Food Traceability List includes ready-to-eat deli salads, but I could not confirm from FDA whether hummus counts. I believe the compliance date was pushed to July 2028 but did not re-check it. Separately, and this is not a rule gap: a critical limit of 212°F internal for 60 minutes is at the boiling point, so the limit may be hard to hit consistently and could produce frequent deviations. Worth confirming with the PCQI (inferred). I did not assess whether acidity or pH is used as a control, since the plan says nothing about it.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.
3. Hazard analysis

4. Preventive controls

growth at cooling and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller 4 hours

RTE environment production run and between products; environmental spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2
monitoring swabs weekly
Sesame allergen Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at Allergen Label matches the formulation sheet;
printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in washdown verified by ATP swab before
the day, followed by full washdown the next non-sesame product
Metal Metal detection of every sealed tub Process Reject at 2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm non-
ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
